body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGsk0H21JgE

Daniel (@dungeondive) moves his science-fiction series into the post-apocalypse with Wreckland Run, Scott Almes's solo-only Fury Road chase game from Renegade. You pick one of four drivers and one of four cars, each with a damage core that ends the game when it's full, along with pre-installed weapons and its own upgrade cards. Then you work through a seven-chapter campaign whose sealed envelopes add enemies, parts, driver skills and, in chapter two, a deck of canyon-route cards with branching choices.

Each round has two halves. In the wreckage phase you roll eight dice and spend them to buy and repair parts, and red dice push your luck because the parts you're welding together might blow up. Barbed wire facing outward makes ramming hurt more. In the run phase Raiders surround your car, red dice trigger their attacks, and up to three white dice fire your weapons. Enemies destroyed exactly, with no excess damage, become scrap you can spend later. The third run brings the warlord boss.

He was more excited at the idea than at the table. When the dice don't cooperate there's little else to do, and the moments of a burning car scraping through on its last six are too rare to match the film's tension. He calls the campaign shoehorned in: a forgettable story, and skills that still cost a die to use. He'd rather it were a roguelite like Mini Rogue or Unbroken, with everything unlocked. The awkward box size seals it: it's leaving his shelf.

----

Daniel thinks Wreckland Run would be better as a roguelite than a campaign. Which small-box games have you felt were held back by a campaign they didn't need?
